STATE CIVIL SERVICE DISCIPLINARY DUE PROCESS (GOVERNMENT CODE §§ 19570-19589) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · California Department of Example Services

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — STATE CIVIL SERVICE DISCIPLINARY DUE PROCESS AT TERMINATION
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as Associate Governmental Program Analyst with California Department of Example Services. This information sheet describes the disciplinary-proceedings article of the State Civil Service Act, California Government Code sections 19570 through 19589 — a chapter of statutes that applies to employees of the California state civil service (agencies and departments under the jurisdiction of the State Personnel Board), and that provides procedural rights connected to a written notice before dismissal, demotion, suspension, or other disciplinary action, the right to file a written answer, the right to a hearing, and administrative and judicial review, separate from the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, the wrongful-termination doctrines, and the general personnel-record statutes this project addresses elsewhere. It is not an answer filed with the State Personnel Board, an administrative appeal, a petition for rehearing, a writ of mandate petition, or a superior court filing, and completing it does not initiate, extend, or preserve any deadline under Government Code section 19574, section 19575, section 19586, or any other statute, board rule, or memorandum of understanding. Completing it does not establish that California Department of Example Services took, or failed to take, any specific action described in this sheet, or that any statement here is true.

SOURCE AND SCOPE: THE STATE CIVIL SERVICE ACT'S DISCIPLINARY-PROCEEDINGS ARTICLE
The rights described in this document come from a specific statutory article — Article 1 (Disciplinary Proceedings) of Chapter 7 (Separations From Service) of Part 2 (State Civil Service) of Division 5 (Personnel) of Title 2 of the Government Code, Government Code sections 19570 through 19589 — not from a general common-law or constitutional theory of public-employee due process. The article's own authorization provision ties any adverse action to two sources: the article itself and the disciplinary rule adopted by the board (the State Personnel Board), and applies to an employee or to a person whose name appears on an employment list, for any cause for discipline the article specifies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In conformity with this article and the board rule, adverse action may be taken against any employee, or person whose name appears on any employment list for any cause for discipline specified in this article."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19571 (California Legislative Information text), authorization for adverse action under the disciplinary-proceedings article (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19571.)
  Known gap: This article is part of the State Civil Service Act and, by its own terms and placement, governs employees within the state civil service under the State Personnel Board's jurisdiction — it does not apply to a private-sector employee, to a peace officer's separate procedural rights under the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act (addressed in a different document in this project), or, without more research this clause does not undertake, necessarily to every category of local-government civil service employee, whose procedural rights typically come instead from a city or county charter, civil-service ordinance, or memorandum of understanding rather than from this state statute. This clause also does not resolve whether a specific appointment is state civil service as opposed to an exempt, at-will, or contract position to which this article does not apply.

THE ARTICLE'S OWN DEFINITION OF "ADVERSE ACTION," AND THE MANAGERIAL-EMPLOYEE EXCLUSION
The article defines its own trigger term. "Adverse action" — the term used throughout the notice, answer, hearing, and appeal provisions described in this document — means dismissal, demotion, suspension, or other disciplinary action. The article carves out a separate category of state employee: it does not apply to an adverse action affecting a managerial employee subject to the separate article governing managerial employees, except to the limited extent three specific cross-referenced sections of that other article say otherwise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "As used in this article “adverse action” means dismissal, demotion, suspension, or other disciplinary action. This article shall not apply to any adverse action affecting managerial employees subject to Article 2 (commencing with Section 19590), except as provided in Sections 19590.5, 19592, and 19592.2."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19570 (California Legislative Information text), definition of "adverse action" and the managerial-employee exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19570.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the definition and the cross-reference itself; it does not independently research or restate what Government Code sections 19590.5, 19592, and 19592.2 (the exceptions to the managerial exclusion) actually provide, or what makes a given position a "managerial employee" under the separate article (commencing with Section 19590) that this section cross-references. Whether a specific classification is treated as managerial for this purpose, and so falls outside this article entirely, is a title- and classification-specific question this clause does not resolve.

THE STATUTE'S OWN LIST OF WHAT CONSTITUTES "CAUSE FOR DISCIPLINE"
Adverse action under this article must rest on one or more of the causes for discipline the statute itself enumerates — an employer using this article is not free to discipline for any reason at all. The statute lists 24 lettered causes, opening with fraud in securing appointment, incompetency, and inefficiency, and continuing through categories such as inexcusable neglect of duty, insubordination, dishonesty, inexcusable absence without leave, conviction of a felony or a misdemeanor involving moral turpitude, discourteous treatment of the public or other employees, willful disobedience, misuse of state property, unlawful discrimination or harassment on a basis listed in the Fair Employment and Housing Act, and unlawful retaliation against an employee or member of the public who reports a suspected legal violation to the Attorney General or another appropriate authority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Each of the following constitutes cause for discipline of an employee, or of a person whose name appears on any employment list:(a) Fraud in securing appointment.(b) Incompetency.(c) Inefficiency."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19572 (California Legislative Information text), the 24 enumerated causes for discipline (introductory sentence and causes (a) through (c) quoted) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19572.)
  Known gap: This clause's quoted citation reproduces only the introductory sentence and the first three lettered causes (a) through (c) verbatim; the remaining causes, (d) through (x), are described narratively above rather than quoted exactly. In the raw fetched HTML, leginfo renders each lettered subdivision abutting the next with a non-breaking space (not a regular space) immediately after each subdivision's parenthetical letter, and with no space at all between one subdivision's closing period and the next subdivision's opening parenthesis (for example, the source reads ‘appointment.(b)Incompetency.(c)Inefficiency.’ with a non-breaking space consumed after each letter but none before it) — this was verified byte-for-byte in the raw HTML from both fetches and is preserved exactly, non-breaking spaces included, in the quoted text rather than corrected. This clause does not determine whether any specific conduct meets one of these 24 statutory causes, and does not address the separate disciplinary criteria a department may adopt under Government Code section 19573.

THE PRE-DISCIPLINE WRITTEN NOTICE: ITS FIVE REQUIRED CONTENTS AND 15-DAY BOARD FILING DEADLINE
Before adverse action against a covered employee becomes valid, the appointing power (or its authorized representative) must serve the employee, personally or by mail, with a written notice, prior to the action's effective date, containing five specific elements: a statement of the nature of the adverse action; the action's effective date; a statement of the reasons for it in ordinary language; a statement advising the employee of the right to answer the notice orally or in writing; and a statement advising the employee of the time within which an appeal must be filed. The appointing power must separately file the notice with the board no later than 15 calendar days after the adverse action's effective date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The appointing power, or its authorized representative, may take adverse action against an employee for one or more of the causes for discipline specified in this article. Adverse action is valid only if a written notice is served on the employee prior to the effective date of the action, as defined by board rule. The notice shall be served upon the employee either personally or by mail and shall include: (1) a statement of the nature of the adverse action; (2) the effective date of the action; (3) a statement of the reasons therefor in ordinary language; (4) a statement advising the employee of the right to answer the notice orally or in writing; and (5) a statement advising the employee of the time within which an appeal must be filed. The notice shall be filed with the board not later than 15 calendar days after the effective date of the adverse action."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19574(a) (California Legislative Information text), the five required contents of the pre-adverse-action written notice and the 15-day board-filing deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19574.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of the statute; subdivision (b), which materially narrows who this subdivision currently reaches, is addressed in a separate clause of this document and should be read together with this one before assuming this notice procedure applies to a given state employee. The statute leaves "as defined by board rule" undefined here — the precise administrative timing of when a notice must be served "prior to the effective date of the action" depends on a State Personnel Board rule this clause does not independently look up or quote. This clause also does not address what happens, or what remedy is available, if a notice omits one of the five required elements or is filed with the board late.

A MAJOR LIMITATION: SUBDIVISION (A)'S NOTICE RULE IS NOW CONFINED TO STATE BARGAINING UNIT 5, AND A MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING CAN OVERRIDE THE HEARING RULES
The same section that states the five-element notice requirement also narrows it: effective January 1, 1996, subdivision (b) states that subdivision (a) shall apply only to state employees in State Bargaining Unit 5, and that the section does not apply to discipline as defined by a separate section, 19576.1. A related section elsewhere in this article makes the same point about a memorandum of understanding generally: if a memorandum of understanding reached under the State Employer-Employee Relations Act conflicts with this article's provisions on whether a hearing must be held, the memorandum of understanding controls without further legislative action, unless it would require an expenditure of funds not approved by the Legislature in the annual Budget Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) Effective January 1, 1996, this subdivision shall apply only to state employees in State Bargaining Unit 5. This section shall not apply to discipline as defined by Section 19576.1."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19574(b) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (b)'s State Bargaining Unit 5 limitation on subdivision (a)'s notice rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19574.)
  "If the provisions of this section concerning whether a hearing should be held are in conflict with the provisions of a memorandum of understanding reached pursuant to the State Employer-Employee Relations Act (SEERA), commencing with Section 3512, the memorandum of understanding shall be controlling without further legislative action, except that if those provisions of a memorandum of understanding require the expenditure of funds, the provisions shall not become effective unless approved by the Legislature in the annual Budget Act."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19576 (California Legislative Information text), a memorandum of understanding's power to override this article's hearing rules (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19576.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b) exactly as codified, but the subdivision's own wording is ambiguous on its face about whether "this subdivision" in its first sentence means subdivision (a) (the notice requirement) or subdivision (b) itself; this clause does not resolve that ambiguity and instead flags it so a reader does not assume subdivision (a)'s notice procedure applies to their own bargaining unit without checking. This clause also does not identify which state employees fall within "State Bargaining Unit 5" (historically the California Highway Patrol's bargaining unit) as opposed to the many other state bargaining units, does not reproduce the separate definition of "discipline" in Government Code section 19576.1 that this subdivision cross-references, and does not identify the specific memorandum of understanding, if any, that actually governs a given reader's adverse-action procedure in place of this article's default rules — that document, not this information sheet, controls in case of conflict.

THE 30-DAY DEADLINE TO FILE A WRITTEN ANSWER, AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF MISSING IT
An employee who receives a notice of adverse action has 30 calendar days after the action's effective date to file a written answer with the board. The answer is treated as denying every allegation in the notice not expressly admitted, and as a request for a hearing or investigation under this article. With the board's or its authorized representative's consent, the employee may later file an amended answer. If the employee does not answer within the 30-day period, or later withdraws the appeal after answering, the adverse action taken by the appointing power becomes final.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employee has 30 calendar days after the effective date of the adverse action to file with the board a written answer to the notice of adverse action. The answer shall be deemed to be a denial of all of the allegations of the notice of adverse action not expressly admitted and a request for hearing or investigation as provided in this article. With the consent of the board or its authorized representative an amended answer may subsequently be filed. If the employee fails to answer within the time specified or after answer withdraws his or her appeal the adverse action taken by the appointing power shall be final."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19575 (California Legislative Information text), the 30-calendar-day deadline to file a written answer and the finality consequence of missing it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19575.)
  Known gap: This clause does not address whether, or under what circumstances, the 30-day period can be extended or excused (for example, for a late-discovered notice defect), and does not address how a partial or ambiguous answer is treated beyond the statute's own default rule that an unadmitted allegation is deemed denied. It also does not describe the format an answer must take or where or how it must be filed with the board beyond what this section itself states, and does not address whether a period shorter than 30 days for an employee to answer could ever be substituted by an applicable memorandum of understanding, a question this clause does not research.

THE RIGHT TO A HEARING ONCE AN ANSWER IS FILED, AND HOW IT MUST BE CONDUCTED
Once an employee files an answer to a notice of adverse action, the board or its authorized representative must, within a reasonable time, hold a hearing (subject to the separate, narrower investigation-only procedure this article allows for certain minor discipline). The board must notify the parties of the hearing's time and place. The hearing itself must be conducted under the Government Code's general administrative-adjudication procedure section governing agency hearings, except that witness examination follows this article's own separate section on examination, and the parties may submit all proper and competent evidence for or against the stated causes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in Section 19576, whenever an answer is filed to an adverse action, the board or its authorized representative shall within a reasonable time hold a hearing. The board shall notify the parties of the time and place of the hearing. The hearing shall be conducted in accordance with the provisions of Section 11513 of the Government Code, except that the employee and other persons may be examined as provided in Section 19580, and the parties may submit all proper and competent evidence against or in support of the causes."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19578 (California Legislative Information text), the right to a hearing once an answer is filed and the applicable hearing procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19578.)
  Known gap: This clause does not independently look up or restate what Government Code section 11513 (the cross-referenced general hearing-procedure statute) itself requires, or what the narrower investigation-only procedure under Government Code section 19576 covers and how it differs from a full hearing — those are addressed, if at all, elsewhere in this project or not at this depth. It also does not address the employee's right (if any) to be represented by counsel or a union representative at the hearing, a topic this section's text does not itself state and that this clause does not research further.

THE BOARD'S DECISION STANDARD, AND HOW BACKPAY AND BENEFITS ARE CALCULATED (AND REDUCED) IF THE ACTION IS REVERSED
After the hearing or investigation, the board must render a decision within a reasonable time; the adverse action stands unless the board modifies or revokes it. If the board finds the stated cause or causes insufficient or not sustained, or that the employee's conduct was justified, it may modify or revoke the action and order the employee returned to the position, with appropriate restoration of backpay and lost benefits as of the adverse action's date or a later date the board specifies. When the board does revoke or modify an adverse action this way, it must direct payment of salary and accrued interest and reinstate all benefits that otherwise would have normally accrued. But that backpay obligation has real limits: salary is not authorized for any period the employee was not ready, able, and willing to perform the position's duties (whether or not the adverse action itself was valid), and the statute requires an offset — from any salary due, the board must deduct compensation the employee earned, or reasonably could have earned, for any period beginning more than six months after the suspension's initial date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The board shall render a decision within a reasonable time after the hearing or investigation. The adverse action taken by the appointing power shall stand unless modified or revoked by the board. If the board finds that the cause or causes for which the adverse action was imposed were insufficient or not sustained, or that the employee was justified in the course of conduct upon which the causes were based, it may modify or revoke the adverse action and it may order the employee returned to his or her position with appropriate restoration of backpay and lost benefits either as of the date of the adverse action or as of such later date as it may specify."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19583 (California Legislative Information text), the board's decision standard and its authority to order backpay and restoration of lost benefits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19583.)
  "Whenever the board revokes or modifies an adverse action and orders that the employee be returned to his or her position, it shall direct the payment of salary and all interest accrued thereto, and the reinstatement of all benefits that otherwise would have normally accrued."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text), the board's duty to direct payment of salary, interest, and reinstated benefits when it reverses or modifies an adverse action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19584.)
  "Salary shall not be authorized or paid for any portion of a period of adverse action that the employee was not ready, able, and willing to perform the duties of his or her position, whether the adverse action is valid or not or the causes on which it is based state facts sufficient to constitute cause for discipline."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text), the limitation that salary is not payable for a period the employee was not ready, able, and willing to work (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19584.)
  "From any such salary due there shall be deducted compensation that the employee earned, or might reasonably have earned, during any period commencing more than six months after the initial date of the suspension."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text), the mitigation offset for compensation earned, or reasonably earned, more than six months after the suspension began (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19584.)
  Known gap: This clause does not resolve fact-specific questions such as what counts as being "ready, able, and willing" to perform the position's duties during a disputed period, or what amount of substitute earnings a board would treat as having been "reasonably" earned for purposes of the six-month offset rule — both are case-specific determinations for the board to make on the evidence, not a formula this clause supplies. It also does not address the separate constitutional-discretion cross-reference this same section (19583) makes to Article VII, Section 3 of the California Constitution and to Government Code section 19573's disciplinary criteria, an aspect of the decision standard this clause does not quote or analyze further.

PETITIONING THE BOARD FOR REHEARING, AND THE SEPARATE, PRESERVED RIGHT TO SEEK JUDICIAL REVIEW
After the board serves its decision, either party has 30 days to petition the board in writing for rehearing, stating all grounds on which rehearing should be granted. Separately, and importantly, the statute preserves an employee's right to petition a court for a writ of mandate, or to bring or maintain any action or proceeding based on or related to any civil service law of California or its administration — that right is not affected by a failure to first petition the board for rehearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Within 30 days after the day a copy of the decision rendered by the board in a proceeding under this article is served by the board upon the parties to the decision, either party may petition the board for rehearing of the decision. The petition for rehearing shall be in writing and shall contain all of the grounds upon which a rehearing should be granted."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19586 (California Legislative Information text), the 30-day deadline to petition the board for rehearing of its decision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19586.)
  "The right to petition a court for writ of mandate, or to bring or maintain any action or proceeding based on or related to any civil service law of this State or the administration thereof shall not be affected by the failure to apply for rehearing by filing written petition therefor with the board."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19588 (California Legislative Information text), the preserved right to petition a court for a writ of mandate regardless of whether rehearing was sought (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19588.)
  Known gap: This clause does not address the statutory deadline for filing a writ of mandate petition in superior court itself (a question of the Code of Civil Procedure this project may address elsewhere, if at all, but that this clause does not research or cite here), does not describe the standard of judicial review a court applies to the board's decision, and does not address the separate 90-day deadline this article's rehearing section imposes on the board to act on a rehearing petition once filed (addressed only in the board's own procedural timeline, not the employee's filing deadline, and not fully quoted in this clause).

LETTERS OF REPRIMAND MUST BE REMOVED FROM THE PERSONNEL FILE AND DESTROYED AFTER THREE YEARS
Separately from the adverse-action notice, answer, and hearing process, this article requires that a letter of reprimand be removed from the state employee's personnel file and destroyed no later than three years from the date the letter was issued.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Letters of reprimand shall be removed from the personnel file of the state employee and destroyed not later than three years from the date the letters were issued."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 19589 (California Legislative Information text), the three-year removal-and-destruction requirement for letters of reprimand (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=19589.)
  Known gap: This clause does not address whether or how an employee can request or enforce this removal if an agency fails to act after three years, does not address whether the underlying facts described in a removed reprimand letter can still be referenced from other agency records or in a later disciplinary action, and does not address the retention rules for any other type of personnel record (such as a notice of adverse action itself or investigative material) which are not covered by this specific three-year reprimand-letter rule.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — STATE CIVIL SERVICE DISCIPLINARY DUE PROCESS INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 6, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes Article 1 (Disciplinary Proceedings) of Chapter 7 of Part 2 of the State Civil Service Act, California Government Code sections 19570, 19571, 19572, 19574, 19575, 19576, 19578, 19583, 19584, 19586, 19588, and 19589 — the article's definitions of "adverse action" and its enumerated causes for discipline, the five-element pre-action written notice and its current State Bargaining Unit 5 limitation, the 30-day right to answer, the right to a hearing, the board's decision standard and backpay/mitigation rules if an action is reversed or modified, the right to petition for rehearing, the separately preserved right to seek judicial review by writ of mandate, and the three-year reprimand-letter removal rule. It does not itself determine that California Department of Example Services did, or did not, comply with any provision of this article with respect to Jordan Lee, is not an answer, administrative appeal, petition for rehearing, writ of mandate petition, or court filing, is not filed with any agency or court by completing it, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, the employing agency's own board rules or applicable memorandum of understanding, or a licensed attorney.]

The notice shall be served upon the employee either personally or by mail and shall include: (1) a statement of the nature of the adverse action; (2) the effective date of the action; (3) a statement of the reasons therefor in ordinary language; (4) a statement advising the employee of the right to answer the notice orally or in writing; and (5) a statement advising the employee of the time within which an appeal must be filed. The notice shall be filed with the board not later than 15 calendar days after the effective date of the adverse action.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of the statute; subdivision (b), which materially narrows who this subdivision currently reaches, is addressed in a separate clause of this document and should be read together with this one before assuming this notice procedure applies to a given state employee. The statute leaves "as defined by board rule" undefined here — the precise administrative timing of when a notice must be served "prior to the effective date of the action" depends on a State Personnel Board rule this clause does not independently look up or quote. This clause also does not address what happens, or what remedy is available, if a notice omits one of the five required elements or is filed with the board late.

expectedJSON.body: The same section that states the five-element notice requirement also narrows it: effective January 1, 1996, subdivision (b) states that subdivision (a) shall apply only to state employees in State Bargaining Unit 5, and that the section does not apply to discipline as defined by a separate section, 19576.1. A related section elsewhere in this article makes the same point about a memorandum of understanding generally: if a memorandum of understanding reached under the State Employer-Employee Relations Act conflicts with this article's provisions on whether a hearing must be held, the memorandum of understanding controls without further legislative action, unless it would require an expenditure of funds not approved by the Legislature in the annual Budget Act.

citations.quote: If the provisions of this section concerning whether a hearing should be held are in conflict with the provisions of a memorandum of understanding reached pursuant to the State Employer-Employee Relations Act (SEERA), commencing with Section 3512, the memorandum of understanding shall be controlling without further legislative action, except that if those provisions of a memorandum of understanding require the expenditure of funds, the provisions shall not become effective unless approved by the Legislature in the annual Budget Act.

This clause also does not identify which state employees fall within "State Bargaining Unit 5" (historically the California Highway Patrol's bargaining unit) as opposed to the many other state bargaining units, does not reproduce the separate definition of "discipline" in Government Code section 19576.1 that this subdivision cross-references, and does not identify the specific memorandum of understanding, if any, that actually governs a given reader's adverse-action procedure in place of this article's default rules — that document, not this information sheet, controls in case of conflict.

expectedJSON.body: An employee who receives a notice of adverse action has 30 calendar days after the action's effective date to file a written answer with the board. The answer is treated as denying every allegation in the notice not expressly admitted, and as a request for a hearing or investigation under this article. With the board's or its authorized representative's consent, the employee may later file an amended answer. If the employee does not answer within the 30-day period, or later withdraws the appeal after answering, the adverse action taken by the appointing power becomes final.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19575 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 30-calendar-day deadline to file a written answer and the finality consequence of missing it
citations.quote: The employee has 30 calendar days after the effective date of the adverse action to file with the board a written answer to the notice of adverse action. The answer shall be deemed to be a denial of all of the allegations of the notice of adverse action not expressly admitted and a request for hearing or investigation as provided in this article. With the consent of the board or its authorized representative an amended answer may subsequently be filed. If the employee fails to answer within the time specified or after answer withdraws his or her appeal the adverse action taken by the appointing power shall be final.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not address whether, or under what circumstances, the 30-day period can be extended or excused (for example, for a late-discovered notice defect), and does not address how a partial or ambiguous answer is treated beyond the statute's own default rule that an unadmitted allegation is deemed denied. It also does not describe the format an answer must take or where or how it must be filed with the board beyond what this section itself states, and does not address whether a period shorter than 30 days for an employee to answer could ever be substituted by an applicable memorandum of understanding, a question this clause does not research.

expectedJSON.body: Once an employee files an answer to a notice of adverse action, the board or its authorized representative must, within a reasonable time, hold a hearing (subject to the separate, narrower investigation-only procedure this article allows for certain minor discipline). The board must notify the parties of the hearing's time and place. The hearing itself must be conducted under the Government Code's general administrative-adjudication procedure section governing agency hearings, except that witness examination follows this article's own separate section on examination, and the parties may submit all proper and competent evidence for or against the stated causes.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19578 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the right to a hearing once an answer is filed and the applicable hearing procedure
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 19576, whenever an answer is filed to an adverse action, the board or its authorized representative shall within a reasonable time hold a hearing. The board shall notify the parties of the time and place of the hearing. The hearing shall be conducted in accordance with the provisions of Section 11513 of the Government Code, except that the employee and other persons may be examined as provided in Section 19580, and the parties may submit all proper and competent evidence against or in support of the causes.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not independently look up or restate what Government Code section 11513 (the cross-referenced general hearing-procedure statute) itself requires, or what the narrower investigation-only procedure under Government Code section 19576 covers and how it differs from a full hearing — those are addressed, if at all, elsewhere in this project or not at this depth. It also does not address the employee's right (if any) to be represented by counsel or a union representative at the hearing, a topic this section's text does not itself state and that this clause does not research further.

expectedJSON.body: After the hearing or investigation, the board must render a decision within a reasonable time; the adverse action stands unless the board modifies or revokes it. If the board finds the stated cause or causes insufficient or not sustained, or that the employee's conduct was justified, it may modify or revoke the action and order the employee returned to the position, with appropriate restoration of backpay and lost benefits as of the adverse action's date or a later date the board specifies. When the board does revoke or modify an adverse action this way, it must direct payment of salary and accrued interest and reinstate all benefits that otherwise would have normally accrued. But that backpay obligation has real limits: salary is not authorized for any period the employee was not ready, able, and willing to perform the position's duties (whether or not the adverse action itself was valid), and the statute requires an offset — from any salary due, the board must deduct compensation the employee earned, or reasonably could have earned, for any period beginning more than six months after the suspension's initial date.

citations.quote: The board shall render a decision within a reasonable time after the hearing or investigation. The adverse action taken by the appointing power shall stand unless modified or revoked by the board. If the board finds that the cause or causes for which the adverse action was imposed were insufficient or not sustained, or that the employee was justified in the course of conduct upon which the causes were based, it may modify or revoke the adverse action and it may order the employee returned to his or her position with appropriate restoration of backpay and lost benefits either as of the date of the adverse action or as of such later date as it may specify.

citations.quote: Whenever the board revokes or modifies an adverse action and orders that the employee be returned to his or her position, it shall direct the payment of salary and all interest accrued thereto, and the reinstatement of all benefits that otherwise would have normally accrued.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: Salary shall not be authorized or paid for any portion of a period of adverse action that the employee was not ready, able, and willing to perform the duties of his or her position, whether the adverse action is valid or not or the causes on which it is based state facts sufficient to constitute cause for discipline.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: From any such salary due there shall be deducted compensation that the employee earned, or might reasonably have earned, during any period commencing more than six months after the initial date of the suspension.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not resolve fact-specific questions such as what counts as being "ready, able, and willing" to perform the position's duties during a disputed period, or what amount of substitute earnings a board would treat as having been "reasonably" earned for purposes of the six-month offset rule — both are case-specific determinations for the board to make on the evidence, not a formula this clause supplies. It also does not address the separate constitutional-discretion cross-reference this same section (19583) makes to Article VII, Section 3 of the California Constitution and to Government Code section 19573's disciplinary criteria, an aspect of the decision standard this clause does not quote or analyze further.

expectedJSON.body: After the board serves its decision, either party has 30 days to petition the board in writing for rehearing, stating all grounds on which rehearing should be granted. Separately, and importantly, the statute preserves an employee's right to petition a court for a writ of mandate, or to bring or maintain any action or proceeding based on or related to any civil service law of California or its administration — that right is not affected by a failure to first petition the board for rehearing.

citations.quote: Within 30 days after the day a copy of the decision rendered by the board in a proceeding under this article is served by the board upon the parties to the decision, either party may petition the board for rehearing of the decision. The petition for rehearing shall be in writing and shall contain all of the grounds upon which a rehearing should be granted.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the adverse-action notice, answer, and hearing process, this article requires that a letter of reprimand be removed from the state employee's personnel file and destroyed no later than three years from the date the letter was issued.
